summary: Describes policy-based accounting, an approach that gives accounting architectures flexibility by expressing their configuration as standardized policies. These can be exchanged between AAA entities to share configuration. It presents building blocks and message sequences. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: Counting who used how much of a service can be done in many ways. This document suggests writing the counting rules as shareable instructions so different systems can set themselves up alike.

questions: how do aaa servers share accounting configuration
how can i outsource network accounting
what is the difference between integrated and discrete accounting
subtitle: Use standardized policies to configure how a network measures and counts resource usage.

tldr.problem: Network service providers have different charging schemes, metering equipment, and inter-domain needs. Manually configuring accounting for each scenario is inflexible and prevents sharing of configuration across heterogeneous systems.
tldr.mechanism: Accounting policies describe rules for metering, collection, and storage of resource consumption data in a standardized way. AAA servers exchange these policies to configure meters and accounting systems, allowing the same policies to work across different equipment.
tldr.outcome: Providers can dynamically adapt their accounting infrastructure to business models and share configuration with roaming partners, and can outsource or delegate accounting functions while maintaining consistent behavior.

today: RFC 3334 is an Experimental protocol from 2002. While it describes a sound approach to standardizing accounting configuration, it has not become an Internet Standard. Modern networks often use DiffServ-based accounting, NetFlow, or sFlow for traffic measurement. Policy-based approaches have been adopted in specific domains such as quality-of-service provisioning and mobile networks, but a unified policy language and framework for accounting across all provider types remains an area of ongoing research.

sections.title: Problem and Approach
sections.content:
Accounting collects data about network resource consumption for charging and billing. Service providers have different needs: some charge per volume, others per time or per service class. They use different metering equipment (NeTraMet, NetFlow, or custom systems) and have heterogeneous infrastructure. Configuring each system separately is inflexible, especially across domain boundaries.

Policy-based accounting addresses this by expressing accounting configuration as standardized policies that can be exchanged between Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) servers. A policy describes conditions (such as user ID, service class, or time of day) and corresponding actions (such as which attributes to measure, how often to report, and where to send records). The same policy can be translated into different configurations for NeTraMet meters, NetFlow collectors, or other systems.
sections.eli5: Instead of telling each piece of equipment differently how to count, you write the rules once in a standard way, and each piece of equipment translates that into its own language.

sections.title: Reference Model and Building Blocks
sections.content:
The RFC describes accounting as a layered process from bottom to top: Metering captures raw data about traffic (volume, source, destination, time). Collection gathers meter data via push (meter reports) or pull (collector requests). Accounting associates the collected data with users and customers, control what data is collected and stored. Charging applies tariffs to accounting data to derive costs. Billing converts costs into invoices and statements.

Policies configure the metering and collection layers. Higher-level policies can be translated into lower-level policies specific to the equipment. For example, a metering policy specifies which flows to measure and what granularity, which influences how a meter is configured. A collection policy specifies whether data is pulled or pushed and how often, influencing collector behavior.
sections.eli5: You measure the traffic, collect what you measured, organize the data, apply prices, and make a bill. Policies control the measuring and collecting steps.

sections.title: Policies, Conditions, and Actions
sections.content:
An accounting policy is a set of rules, each with a condition and an action. The condition specifies when the rule applies using attributes like customer ID, IP address, time of day, service class, or accounting type. For example, a condition might be "all users in service class gold during business hours."

The action specifies what happens: configuration of the accounting infrastructure such as which attributes to measure, what record type to use, report intervals, storage duration, and access permissions. A provider might configure detailed, frequent reporting for premium customers and minimal reporting for basic customers using policies with the same structure.

Policies can be pushed (sent from one AAA server to another to enforce locally) or pulled (requested from a partner when needed). The RFC does not propose a specific policy language but assumes standardized formats like COPS-PR or SNMP can be used to implement policy decisions.
sections.eli5: A policy is a rule: "if this condition is true, then do this action." For example, "if the customer is premium, then measure every single packet and report every minute."

sections.title: Integrated and Discrete Accounting
sections.content:
The RFC describes two approaches: Integrated accounting couples accounting to a specific service. The accounting configuration is part of service provisioning, tailored to that service's equipment (e.g., using SIP signaling information for VoIP call accounting). The Application Specific Module (ASM) converts generic accounting policies from the AAA server into service-specific configuration.

Discrete accounting treats accounting as a separate, general service. A single accounting provider can measure traffic for multiple services and service providers. This allows outsourcing: a provider requests accounting service and receives back accounting records without managing meters themselves. The same metering setup can support different services and charging schemes.

Intra-domain accounting occurs within one administrative domain with no policy exchange needed. Inter-domain accounting involves roaming or multi-provider scenarios where one provider collects data (foreign provider) and another applies charges (home provider). The home provider sends accounting policies to the foreign provider to specify what data to collect.
sections.eli5: Accounting can be built into a service (like using call signaling for VoIP charges) or be a separate service that counts for anything (like an independent meter company).

sections.title: Real-World Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC provides examples of policy-based accounting in action. In a printing service scenario, the home provider sends an accounting policy to a foreign provider requesting detailed records of file transfers and print jobs at specific intervals. The foreign provider either confirms it can enforce the policy or denies it if its equipment cannot measure the requested attributes or meet the reporting frequency.

In roaming (mobile user scenario), a home provider that bills the user sends an accounting policy to a foreign provider to configure how traffic is metered and how often records are sent. In DiffServ scenarios, providers use policies to configure meters to measure traffic per differentiated services code point (DSCP). Policies allow users or providers to request accounting indications (interim usage reports) so they can monitor consumption and avoid bill shock.

These scenarios show that policy-based accounting enables flexible, inter-domain resource management without requiring each provider to duplicate metering infrastructure.
sections.eli5: A company can tell its roaming partner "I want to know how much data my employees used, broken down by service type, every hour." The roaming partner sets its meters to provide exactly that.
